newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Vranitzky says fascism never again.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Vranitzky says fascism never again.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky urged voters on Friday to reject the far right in European parliamentary and Vienna state elections next week, saying fascism should never take hold in Austria again.

Support for Vranitzky's Social Democrats has slipped in the polls and political analysts predict the party will lose its majority control of the powerful Vienna city council for the first time since 1945.

The far-right Freedom Party has gained backing in polls and could take 25 percent of the vote in the European election on October 13 and consolidate its position as the second biggest party in the Austrian capital.

Speaking at a rally in the northern industrial town of Linz, Vranitzky took a swipe at right leader Joerg Haider, who he said relied on slogans and glamorous public relations gimmicks instead of listening to Austrian voters.
"Let us be responsible about the far-right fringe. We must never again let fascism have a future in our country," the chancellor said to loud applause.
Fascists seized control in 1934, four years before Adolf Hitler annexed Austria into the Third Reich.
Haider has played on voter fears of job losses and anger over benefit cuts, blaming European Union policies and the annual net contribution Austria makes to Brussels coffers.

Vranitzky arrived at the rally in a railway works in Linz flanked by bodyguards. Security around the chancellor has been tightened after he was named as a target in a threat by suspected right-wing extremists to blow up prominent people in Austria and abroad.

A group calling itself the Bajuvarian Liberation Army warned it planned to target eight well-known figures in a renewed offensive. The group has claimed responsibility for over 20 letter bombs directed against foreigners and figures linked to immigrant or refugee issues since 1993.
Outlining his party's goals in Europe, Vranitzky said the fight against unemployment was a top priority.
"We want a strong voice in Europe to stop savings measures that only go towards cutting jobs," he said.
Vranitzky, who leaves for a special EU summit in Dublin on Saturday, said Austria had benefited from lower inflation and higher exports since its entry into the EU in January 1995.
Besides employment, the chancellor stressed that EU membership did not mean Austria would lose its neutrality.

"I don't believe we have to solve problems through a military pact. I prefer to prevent them by building up an efficient (European) security structure so that we do not need military operations," he said.
